title: Adapter and Facade
goal: By the end you can wrap a vendor SDK in an adapter that keeps its types, codes and exceptions to itself, use Kotlin extension functions for light data adapters, and put a multi-step checkout behind a facade that owns the order and the failure rules.

warmup.q: A Kotlin adapter implements `fun interface Gateway { fun charge(amountMinor: Long): String }` and calls a vendor method that throws `IOException`, with no try/catch. What happens when the vendor throws?
options: It doesn't compile: the `IOException` must be caught or declared
The `IOException` travels straight through the port to whoever called `charge`
Kotlin wraps it in an `UndeclaredThrowableException`
The exception is swallowed and `charge` returns an empty string
warmup.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the code compiles and the vendor's `IOException` reaches your service code through a port that never mentioned it. In Java the same adapter would not compile, because the port's method doesn't declare `IOException`. Translating vendor errors at the boundary is a habit you need in Kotlin.

sections.h: Ports and adapters: where the translation lives
sections.body:
Adapter and Facade both wrap something, and so do Decorator, Proxy and Bridge. Structure won't tell them apart. Intent will:

| Pattern | Wraps | Offers | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adapter | one object you can't change | a different interface: yours | make it fit your port |
| Facade | several objects | a new, simpler interface | hide a sequence of calls |
| Decorator | one object | the same interface | add behavior (*Decorator and Proxy*, lesson 5 of this track) |
| Proxy | one object | the same interface | control access (lesson 5 of this track) |
| Bridge | an implementation you pick | your abstraction | vary two dimensions (lesson 6 of this track) |

In a service built with ports and adapters (often called hexagonal architecture), you see Adapter and Facade on one picture. The payment logic sits in the middle and talks only to ports: `CardAuthorizer`, `Ledger`, `Notifier`. Adapters sit on the edge, one per technology: the issuer SDK adapter, an Oracle ledger, a Kafka notifier. The facade is the front door, where a REST resource or a Kafka consumer makes one call.

That layout pays off twice. Switching issuers means writing one new adapter, and nothing in the middle changes. And the middle is tested with lambdas: `new CheckoutFacade((pan, amount, currency) -> new Approved("A1"), ledger, notifier)` needs no SDK, no database and no broker.

Domain-driven design calls a thick layer of adapters an anti-corruption layer: the place where the vendor's model (response code "51", numeric currency "978", amounts as strings) is translated into yours, so it never spreads. If you find `"51"` in a service class, the layer has a hole. The lab is that layer in miniature: an adapter that keeps an issuer SDK's quirks to itself, and a facade that callers can use without knowing the steps.

figure.caption: Callers make one call to the facade. Your code talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge translate to each vendor.

analogy: An adapter is the travel plug you carry abroad: the hotel's socket stays the same, your charger stays the same, and the plug translates between them. A facade is the hotel's front desk: you ask for a taxi to the airport at six, and the desk deals with the taxi company, the wake-up call and the bill. You never call the taxi company yourself. The analogy breaks on errors: a travel plug either fits or it doesn't, but a software adapter must also translate the vendor's failures into yours, and a leaky one passes the foreign voltage straight through.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus services already have ports and adapters, even if nobody calls them that: a REST client interface for a PSP, a `@ApplicationScoped` bean that wraps the issuer SDK, a Kafka emitter behind a `Notifier`. Check where the vendor's vocabulary ends. A response code "05" in a Temporal activity, or a vendor exception caught in a REST resource, means the adapter is leaking. Temporal makes this concrete: activity retry policies decide on exception types, so translate vendor errors into your own retryable and non-retryable exceptions inside the adapter, where you know which is which. And a checkout facade is a natural Temporal workflow later, once the steps need durable retries.
mistake: The most common mistake is the leaky adapter: it wraps the vendor's method calls but lets the vendor's model through. The adapter rethrows `SdkException` (or wraps it in a `RuntimeException` that callers unwrap), returns the vendor's response code as a string, or exposes the vendor's DTOs in its method signatures. It happens because translating every code and error feels like busywork when there is only one vendor. Then the second issuer arrives, and every service that checks `"51"` has to change. Translate everything at the boundary into your own sealed results and exceptions, and test the adapter against a fake of the vendor class.

compare.title: An anti-corruption adapter for a PSP webhook

java.title: PspWebhookAdapter.java

kotlin.title: PspWebhookAdapter.kt

compare.note: The translation is identical: vendor strings in, a sealed event of our own out. Kotlin writes it as an extension on the vendor type, so call sites read `webhook.toEvent()`; Java needs a static method on a holder class, so they read `PspWebhookAdapter.toEvent(webhook)`. In bytecode they are the same static method. Both use a catch-all branch on purpose: vendor event types are an open set you don't control, unlike your own sealed types, where a missing case should break the build. Code that consumes `PaymentEvent` then switches over it with no default. Neither language makes Adapter unnecessary; Kotlin just makes the data-mapping kind cheaper to write.

worked.title: Wrap a vendor FX feed behind a port, then test without it

steps.say: A pricing service calls a vendor FX feed directly. The feed returns strings like `"EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000"` and throws a checked `FeedException`. Before reading on, list every vendor detail that leaks into `priceInUsd`.

Four leaks: the pair format, the response format, the checked exception, and the hard-wired URL. Define the port in your words first. It says nothing about strings or vendors, and an empty result means "no rate right now".

Now the adapter. Everything the vendor knows lives here: how pairs are spelled, how answers are packed, and which exception it throws. Why return empty instead of rethrowing on `FeedException`? Because the port promised "a rate or nothing", and the pricer decides what nothing means.
Test the two halves separately. The pricer gets a lambda. The adapter gets a fake feed, a subclass of the vendor client that returns canned strings, which is how the lab tests its issuer adapter.

lab.title: An issuer SDK adapter and a checkout facade
steps: Read `LegacyIssuerSdk.java`, `CardAuthorizer.java` and `Amounts.java`. They are given; don't edit them. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write `IssuerSdkAdapter.authorize`. Call `sdk.auth` with `Amounts.toDecimal` and `Amounts.numericCode`, catch `SdkException` and return `Unavailable(e.getMessage())`, then split the response on `|` and map the code with a `switch`.

Write `CheckoutFacade.checkout` as a `switch` over the `AuthResult`. Approved: post, send the receipt (catching a failing notifier), return `Paid`. Declined: send the notice, return `Declined`. Unavailable: return `RetryLater`.
Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: `raw.split("\\|", -1)` splits on a literal `|` and keeps the empty auth id in `"51|"`. The pipe must be escaped, because `split` takes a regex.
A `switch` over the sealed `AuthResult` with `case AuthResult.Approved ok -> ...` needs no `default`: the compiler checks all three cases. In a switch expression, use `yield` to return from a block.
Wrap only the notifier call in try/catch. If the ledger post throws, let it propagate: an approved payment that isn't on the ledger is an incident, not something to swallow.

drill.title: An adapter from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A vendor `GeoIpClient` has `String lookup(String ip) throws GeoException`, returning text like `"DE;Berlin"`. Your port is `interface CountryOf { Optional<String> country(String ip); }` (in Kotlin, `fun interface CountryOf { fun country(ip: String): String? }`). Write the adapter so the vendor's exception never escapes and an empty or malformed answer gives no country.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: An adapter makes a class you can't change fit your port. It translates arguments on the way in, and results and errors on the way out.
Keep vendor types, codes and exceptions inside the adapter. A `"51"` or an `SdkException` in a service class is a leak.
Java's checked exceptions stop a vendor `IOException` from escaping a port that doesn't declare it; Kotlin compiles the same leak silently.
For a one-method port, a lambda or a `fun interface` is the adapter. For data mapping in Kotlin, an extension like `VendorTxn.toReceipt()` is the light adapter; in Java it's a static method.
A facade gives callers one call for a multi-step job and owns the order of the steps and what each failure means. Keep it orchestration only.
A Java record component can't be named `notify`, `wait` or another no-argument `Object` method.

quiz.q: Your issuer adapter catches `SdkException` and rethrows it wrapped in a `RuntimeException`. The checkout service catches that and checks `getCause() instanceof SdkException` to decide whether to retry. What's wrong?
options: Nothing, since the exception is unchecked now
The vendor type still leaks: the service depends on the SDK, so switching issuers breaks it
A `RuntimeException` can't wrap a checked exception
Retry decisions belong inside the vendor SDK
quiz.why: Wrapping changed the exception's type, not who depends on it. The service still imports `SdkException`, so it's coupled to this vendor. Translate inside the adapter into your own result (`Unavailable`) or your own exception type that says retryable or not. A `RuntimeException` can wrap anything, so that option is simply false.

quiz.q: Which statement about an adapter written in Kotlin is true?
options: A vendor `IOException` thrown inside it can pass through your port without any compile error
The compiler forces you to catch the vendor's checked exceptions
Extension functions can implement your port interface
`fun interface` ports can't be implemented with a lambda
quiz.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so nothing stops the vendor's `IOException` from reaching callers of your port. Java would refuse to compile the same adapter. Extensions can't implement interfaces, and a `fun interface` exists precisely so a lambda can implement it.

quiz.q: Three call sites (a REST resource, a Kafka consumer and an admin tool) each reserve stock, charge the card, post to the ledger and send an email, each with slightly different failure handling. Which pattern fits?
options: Adapter
Decorator
Facade
Singleton
quiz.why: A facade puts the sequence and its failure rules in one place, and each caller makes one call. An adapter changes one object's interface, a decorator adds behavior behind the same interface, and a singleton is about instance count, not about orchestrating steps.

quiz.q: Which is the best use of a Kotlin extension function as an adapter?
options: `fun LegacyIssuerSdk.authorize(...)`, which callers use instead of a `CardAuthorizer` port
A global `fun Any.toJson()` in a shared utils file
An extension that caches vendor results in a top-level map
`fun VendorTxn.toReceipt(): Receipt`, kept in the issuer-adapter package
quiz.why: Mapping a vendor DTO to your own type is pure data translation, which is what extensions are good at, and keeping it in the adapter package keeps the vendor model contained. An extension on the SDK makes callers depend on the SDK and can't be swapped in a test. A global utils extension spreads everywhere, and caching in a top-level map is hidden shared state.

quiz.q: From *Factory Method and Abstract Factory*: you now have one `IssuerSdkAdapter` for Visa's SDK and one for Mastercard's. Where should the choice between them live?
options: In each REST resource, with an `if` on the card's BIN
In one factory, a `switch` or `when` over the network with no default, injected into the facade
Inside the facade's `checkout`, as string checks on the PAN
In the adapters: each checks whether the card belongs to it
quiz.why: Choosing which product to build is a factory's job: one exhaustive `switch` or `when` over a sealed or enum network, so adding a network is a compile error in one place. Spreading BIN checks over resources or the facade copies the rule, and adapters checking ownership turns every call into a guessing game.

flashcards.back: Makes an object you can't change fit the interface (port) your code expects, translating arguments, results and errors.
One that lets the vendor's types, codes or exceptions (an `SdkException`, response code "51") reach your service code.

flashcards.front: A Kotlin adapter calls a method that throws `IOException` and has no catch. Does it compile?
flashcards.back: Yes. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the vendor's `IOException` passes through your port silently. Java would refuse.

flashcards.front: What does a Kotlin extension function compile to?
flashcards.back: A static method whose first parameter is the receiver. `txn.toReceipt()` is `toReceipt(txn)` in bytecode.
The order of the steps in a multi-step job, and what a failure at each step means. Not maths, vendor codes or SQL.

flashcards.front: Can a Java record component be named `notify`?
flashcards.back: No: "illegal record component name". Its accessor would clash with `Object.notify()`. The same goes for `wait`, `hashCode`, `toString` and the other no-arg `Object` methods.

flashcards.front: Adapter vs Facade, one line each?
flashcards.back: Adapter: one object, given a different interface (yours). Facade: several objects behind one new, simpler interface.

terms.plain: A wrapper that makes an existing object fit the interface your code expects.
An interface in your own words that your core code depends on, such as `CardAuthorizer`.
The adapters where a vendor's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads into your code.
One simple entry point that runs a multi-step job across several subsystems.
A Kotlin function called like a method on a type it doesn't belong to; a static method underneath.
Core logic talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge connect each port to one technology.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a new teammate why `IssuerSdkAdapter` returns `Unavailable` instead of letting `SdkException` through, and why `CheckoutFacade` swallows a failing receipt email but not a failing ledger post.
explain_back.answer: The adapter is the only class allowed to know the issuer's SDK. If `SdkException` escaped, every caller would import the vendor's type and decide on its status codes, and switching issuers would mean changing all of them. So the adapter turns it into our own result, `Unavailable`, and the facade turns that into `RetryLater`. In the facade, the order matters: once the card is approved, the money moved, so the ledger post must happen, and if it fails, that's an incident we must see, so it propagates. The receipt email is best effort. A broken mail server shouldn't turn a completed payment into an error the customer retries, which could charge them twice.

deeper.body:
The JDK has adapters you use daily. `InputStreamReader` adapts a byte stream into a character stream; its Javadoc calls it a bridge from byte streams to character streams, which shows how loosely the pattern names get used. `Arrays.asList` adapts an array into a fixed-size `List` that writes through to the array. `Collections.enumeration` and `Enumeration.asIterator()` (Java 9) adapt between the old and new iteration interfaces.

The GoF book describes two kinds of adapter. An object adapter holds the vendor object and delegates to it, as in this lesson. A class adapter inherits from the vendor class and implements your interface at the same time. Java and Kotlin allow the second only when the vendor class is open, and it is usually worse: your adapter inherits every public method of the SDK, so callers can bypass your translation. Prefer the object adapter.

Kotlin's `by` delegation (in *Decorator and Proxy*, lesson 5 of this track) can build an adapter that forwards most of an interface unchanged and overrides the few methods that need translation. That works when the two interfaces are almost the same, such as two versions of your own API. For a vendor SDK with a different model, write the translation out; it is the part that deserves a review.

Facades and transactions mix badly in one way. If a Spring or Quarkus facade method is `@Transactional` and calls an external issuer inside the transaction, a 120 ms issuer call holds a database connection for 120 ms. With a pool of 20 connections, a slow issuer starves the database. Charge first, outside the transaction, then post to the ledger in a short one, and make the post idempotent so a retry can't double-post.
